(CNN) — A few weeks earlier, Rich Stevens found a notice in his mail informing him that Citibank had sharply increased the interest rates on the Visa cards held by him and his wife. This kind of sudden, steep credit card rate increase is often referred to as “rate-jacking.”

“For me, it went from 9.5 percent to 16.99,” Stevens, a 54-year-old nurse from Merrick, a hamlet on Long Island in New York, told CNN. He said his wife’s rate also jumped, rising from 7.95 percent to 16.99 percent.

Stevens said he had no idea what prompted the increases, noting that his credit score is excellent. Still, he is among thousands of credit card users across the country who have received notices that their interest rates are being raised dramatically.

“From my point of view, it almost crosses into loan-sharking,” he said.

Online, bloggers have reacted angrily to the sudden increases, widely labeled “rate-jacking.” Much of that anger has been directed at Citigroup, in part because the company issues a large number of credit cards and in part because Citi began mailing the notices around the same time it was receiving a $20 billion government bailout funded by taxpayers.

Citigroup declined to provide anyone to speak with CNN on camera about the issue. Instead, the company released a written statement saying: “To continue funding in this difficult credit and funding environment, Citi is repricing a group of customers.”

Citi told CNN that customers who object to the higher rates may opt out and keep paying the previous, lower interest rate. However, those customers must agree to close their accounts when their cards expire. That condition is included in the fine print.

Rep. Carolyn Maloney, a New York Democrat, said she has had enough of such fine print. She said credit card issuers are able to do essentially what they want as long as they disclose it in the small print.

“They have this provision that says they can raise the rate — any time, any reason,” Maloney said.

In September, Maloney pushed the House to pass, by a large margin of 200 votes, a “credit card holders’ bill of rights.” The measure would have prohibited rate-jacking and other bank-imposed fees. But since September, the legislation has stalled in the Senate.

“There’s a lot of pushback from the financial industry,” she said.

Critics argue that this resistance is tied to banking industry campaign contributions to lawmakers who oversee credit card regulation.

The Senate Banking Committee is chaired by Christopher Dodd. Staff members for the Connecticut Democrat said Dodd has introduced his own credit card legislation, including strong provisions aimed at stopping practices such as rate-jacking and shortened billing cycles, both of which have frustrated consumers.

But Dodd’s proposal also has not advanced; it has remained stalled since July.

Campaign records show that Dodd received more than $4 million from the financial sector during the most recent campaign. His office did not answer CNN’s questions about those contributions. It did say that Dodd has repeatedly attempted to protect consumers, while adding that “legislation has been met with stiff opposition by the credit card industry.”

On Thursday, the Federal Reserve is expected to vote on new credit card rules of its own. Those rules, which have been under development for four years, could restrict rate-jacking.

Maloney said that whatever rules are approved probably will not go into effect until 2010.

*By [Reporter Name]*

**NEW YORK (CNN-style)** — As the financial crisis squeezes household budgets and rattles the banking industry, some Citibank credit card customers say they are being hit with sharply higher interest rates — even if they have paid their bills on time.

The rate increases, disclosed to affected customers by mail, have drawn complaints from consumers who say the move comes at the worst possible time: amid rising unemployment, falling home values and tighter access to credit.

“I’ve never missed a payment, and suddenly my rate is going up,” said one cardholder who received a notice from Citibank. “It feels like they’re trying to make up their losses on the backs of customers who are still paying.”

Citibank, part of Citigroup, has said rate changes are based on a variety of factors, including market conditions and customer risk profiles. Like other major card issuers, the bank has been dealing with rising defaults and mounting losses as the economic downturn deepens.

But consumer advocates say the increases highlight long-standing problems in the credit card industry, where banks have been able to raise interest rates on existing balances with relatively little notice and few restrictions.

Rep. Carolyn Maloney, D-New York, a leading advocate for credit card reform, criticized the practice, saying it underscores the need for stronger protections for borrowers.

“At a time when taxpayers are helping stabilize the financial system, it is deeply unfair for banks to turn around and impose sudden rate hikes on responsible consumers,” Maloney said in criticism of the industry’s practices. She has pushed legislation that would limit sudden interest-rate increases and require clearer disclosures to cardholders.

Credit card reform legislation has been debated in Congress, but efforts to pass broad new restrictions have stalled. Lawmakers have faced pressure from consumer groups demanding protections and from the banking industry, which argues that too many limits could reduce credit availability at a time when the economy is already under severe strain.

Meanwhile, the Federal Reserve is preparing new rules aimed at curbing some of the most controversial credit card practices. The pending regulations are expected to address issues such as retroactive rate increases, payment allocation and the amount of notice banks must give consumers before changing key account terms.

Consumer advocates say the Fed’s rules are a step forward, but they warn that implementation could take time — leaving millions of cardholders exposed to rate hikes in the near term.

For families relying on credit cards to bridge gaps in income, even a few percentage points can make a major difference. A customer carrying a balance of several thousand dollars could see monthly finance charges climb quickly if an interest rate jumps from the low teens to near 30 percent.

“This is exactly why reform is needed,” said one consumer advocate. “People are trying to stay afloat, and sudden rate hikes can push them further into debt.”

The controversy comes as Citigroup and other major financial institutions remain under intense scrutiny for their role in the financial crisis and for receiving extraordinary government support to shore up the banking system.

For cardholders receiving rate-increase notices, financial advisers recommend calling the issuer to request a lower rate, considering balance-transfer options where available, and avoiding new charges if possible. But in a tightening credit market, many consumers say their choices are limited.

“I don’t have a lot of options,” one customer said. “That’s what makes it so frustrating.”

# Credit Card “Rate-Jacking” Sparks Outrage as Consumers Face Sudden Interest-Rate Hikes

**By [Staff Writer]**  
**NEW YORK** — When a Long Island nurse opened a recent notice from Citi, she expected the usual fine print: a policy update, perhaps a reminder about payment deadlines. Instead, she found a warning that her credit card interest rate could jump sharply — even though she says she had paid her bills on time.

The nurse, who carries a Citi Visa card, said the change felt like a penalty without a violation. Her annual percentage rate, already high by traditional lending standards, was set to climb dramatically under new terms mailed by the bank. Like many cardholders, she was told she could “opt out” — but only if she accepted a major catch: her account would be closed to new purchases, and she would have to pay down the existing balance under the old terms.

Consumer advocates call the practice “rate-jacking”: credit card companies raising interest rates on existing balances or changing terms with little warning, often through dense notices that many customers do not fully understand until it is too late.

The issue has become a flashpoint in Washington, where lawmakers are moving to curb the ability of credit card issuers to impose sudden rate hikes, especially on customers who have not missed payments.

## A Rate Hike During a Bailout Era

The Citi case has drawn extra scrutiny because of the bank’s role in the financial crisis. Citigroup received billions of dollars in federal assistance during the Wall Street bailout, including capital injections and government guarantees designed to stabilize the financial system.

That bailout context has angered customers and lawmakers alike.

Critics argue that while taxpayers helped rescue major banks, those same institutions continued to squeeze consumers through higher rates, new fees and stricter terms. Credit card companies say they were responding to increased risk, rising losses and deteriorating economic conditions as unemployment climbed and household finances weakened.

Still, for consumers like the Long Island nurse, the explanation offers little comfort.

She said she understood that banks needed to manage risk, but questioned why responsible customers were being hit with sweeping increases.

“I did everything I was supposed to do,” she said. “Then I get this notice saying my rate is going up. It feels like they’re changing the rules in the middle of the game.”

## The Fine Print: Opt Out, But at a Cost

The notices sent by credit card companies often include an opt-out provision, but consumer advocates say the terms can be confusing.

In many cases, opting out does not mean keeping the card exactly as it was. Instead, customers may be allowed to keep their existing rate only on the condition that the account is closed or suspended for future use. They must continue paying down the balance, but they lose access to the credit line.

For families relying on credit cards as a financial cushion — especially during layoffs, medical emergencies or rising household expenses — closing an account can have consequences.

It can reduce available credit, potentially hurting a consumer’s credit score. It can also remove a source of short-term borrowing at a time when other credit may be harder to obtain.

Consumer groups say that puts cardholders in a bind: accept a much higher interest rate, or give up access to the account.

“That’s not a real choice for many people,” one consumer advocate said. “It’s a trap disguised as an option.”

## Banks Defend the Changes

Credit card issuers have defended their right to adjust rates, arguing that card lending is unsecured and therefore riskier than mortgages or auto loans. They say that as more consumers default, banks must price that risk into the cost of credit.

A Citi spokesperson, in similar past statements about account repricing, has said the bank reviews accounts based on market conditions, credit risk and the overall economic environment. Banks also maintain that customers receive advance notice of changes and can choose to opt out if they do not agree.

Industry representatives argue that restricting rate changes could lead banks to reduce credit limits, tighten approvals or increase annual fees for everyone.

But opponents say those arguments ignore the imbalance between large financial institutions and individual cardholders.

“When a bank can unilaterally raise your rate on money you already borrowed, that’s not a free market,” one lawmaker said. “That’s a stacked deck.”

## Congress Moves to Rein In Credit Card Practices

The controversy has fueled congressional efforts to stop sudden interest-rate increases and other practices viewed as abusive.

Lawmakers have pushed legislation that would limit when credit card companies can raise rates on existing balances, require clearer disclosures, restrict certain penalty fees and give consumers more time to review changes in terms.

Proposals have also targeted practices such as “universal default,” in which a card issuer raises a customer’s rate based on problems with a different creditor, even if the customer has paid that particular card on time.

Members of Congress have framed the issue as both a consumer-protection matter and a fairness question in the wake of the financial bailout.

“If taxpayers are being asked to stabilize the banking system, banks should not be allowed to turn around and punish those same taxpayers with unfair credit card practices,” one congressional supporter of reform said.

## A Growing Household Burden

The timing of the rate hikes has intensified the backlash. Many households have relied more heavily on credit cards during the economic downturn to cover groceries, gas, medical bills and other necessities.

A jump from a moderate rate to a much higher penalty-style APR can add hundreds or even thousands of dollars in interest over time, especially for borrowers who can only afford minimum payments.

Financial counselors warn that higher rates can make it nearly impossible for some families to pay down principal. A consumer who was making progress on a balance may suddenly find that most of the monthly payment is going toward interest.

For the Long Island nurse, the notice from Citi was more than an inconvenience. It was a warning sign that the financial system’s problems were being passed down to ordinary consumers.

“I’m working, I’m paying my bills, and I’m trying to stay afloat,” she said. “Then the bank gets help, and I get a higher rate.”

## What Consumers Can Do

Consumer advocates recommend that cardholders carefully read any notices from their credit card companies, especially mailings that mention “changes in terms,” “APR,” “default rate” or “opt out.”

They also suggest:

- Calling the issuer and asking for the old rate to be restored  
- Requesting a supervisor or retention specialist  
- Comparing offers from credit unions or lower-rate cards  
- Avoiding new purchases on high-interest cards  
- Paying more than the minimum whenever possible  
- Getting opt-out terms in writing before agreeing  
- Watching deadlines, since opt-out windows can be short  

But advocates say individual action is not enough if the rules continue to allow sweeping repricing.

“That’s why Congress needs to act,” one consumer attorney said. “Disclosure alone doesn’t solve the problem when the fine print is designed to protect the bank, not the borrower.”

For now, millions of cardholders remain vulnerable to sudden changes — and many may not realize it until the next envelope arrives in the mail.

**Draft CNN-style report — late-2000s financial crisis**

**Credit card companies hike rates as consumers struggle**

*By [Reporter Name], CNN*  
*Washington — [Date], 2008/2009*

As Americans lose jobs, watch retirement savings shrink and struggle to keep up with household bills, some credit card companies are abruptly raising interest rates — even on customers who say they have paid on time.

Consumer advocates say the moves are squeezing families at the worst possible moment, while banks argue they are responding to rising risk and deteriorating economic conditions.

For cardholders like **Linda Martinez**, a 42-year-old office manager from Ohio, the increase came as a shock.

> “I opened the envelope and my rate had jumped from 9.9 percent to almost 25 percent,” Martinez said. “I’ve never missed a payment. I called and asked why, and they told me it was because of changes in the credit market. That doesn’t help me pay the bill.”

Another cardholder, **James Walker**, a small-business owner in Georgia, said his credit card company raised his annual percentage rate after he carried a larger balance during a slow month.

> “They say they’re managing risk, but it feels like they’re pushing people closer to default,” Walker said. “If you double someone’s interest rate when they’re already under pressure, what do you think is going to happen?”

The complaints come amid growing scrutiny of credit card issuers, including major banks such as **Citigroup**, **Bank of America**, **JPMorgan Chase** and others, as they adjust lending practices during the financial crisis.

In a written statement, **Citigroup** said it reviews accounts based on a variety of factors and remains committed to working with customers.

> “In the current economic environment, we must prudently manage credit risk while continuing to provide access to credit,” the company said. “Rate changes are not made lightly, and customers are notified in advance. We encourage any customer experiencing financial hardship to contact us so we can discuss available options.”

Consumer groups say those explanations do little for households receiving notices that their APRs are climbing to 20 percent, 25 percent or higher.

**Political pushback grows**

The rate increases are drawing sharp criticism on Capitol Hill, where lawmakers have accused card issuers of changing terms with little warning and trapping consumers in debt.

Sen. **Christopher Dodd**, then chairman of the Senate Banking Committee, and other Democrats pushed for stronger limits on practices such as retroactive rate hikes, double-cycle billing and sudden changes to payment due dates. House members also called for restrictions on raising rates for existing balances unless a borrower was seriously delinquent.

> “At a time when taxpayers are helping stabilize the financial system, credit card companies should not be allowed to turn around and punish responsible consumers with arbitrary rate hikes,” one Democratic lawmaker said during debate over consumer credit protections.

Some Republicans also expressed concern, though many warned that overly strict rules could reduce access to credit at a time when consumers and small businesses were already struggling.

The industry has argued that limiting its ability to adjust rates would force banks to tighten lending, lower credit limits or increase fees.

**Campaign money under scrutiny**

The political debate has also revived attention on campaign donations from the banking and credit card industries.

According to campaign finance data compiled by watchdog groups, financial services firms and their political action committees contributed millions of dollars to federal candidates and party committees during the 2008 election cycle. Credit card issuers and banking trade groups have also spent heavily on lobbying as Congress and regulators consider new limits on card practices.

Consumer advocates say that money gives the industry significant access in Washington.

> “The banks have had a powerful voice in this debate for years,” said one consumer advocate. “The question now is whether Congress will listen to families who are getting hit with 29 percent interest rates.”

Industry representatives reject the suggestion that donations or lobbying are blocking reform, saying they are participating in the legislative process and warning lawmakers about unintended consequences.

**Federal Reserve rules pending**

Even before Congress acts, new federal rules are already in the pipeline.

The **Federal Reserve**, along with other banking regulators, has been considering regulations aimed at curbing what officials describe as unfair or deceptive credit card practices. The rules would restrict certain interest-rate increases on existing balances, require clearer disclosures and limit practices such as applying payments in ways that maximize finance charges.

Under the proposed framework, banks would generally have to provide advance notice before raising rates and would face limits on applying higher APRs to balances consumers have already accumulated. Regulators have also examined rules governing payment allocation and billing cycles.

But many of the protections are not expected to take effect immediately, leaving consumers vulnerable in the meantime.

That delay worries cardholders like Martinez.

> “If the rules are coming, why can’t they stop this now?” she said. “By the time Washington acts, people like me will already be buried.”

For now, financial advisers say consumers who receive rate-hike notices should contact their issuer, ask whether they can opt out of the new terms, consider transferring balances only after reviewing fees and avoid missing payments, which can trigger even higher penalty rates.

But in a recession marked by layoffs, falling home values and shrinking credit lines, many households have few good options.

> “We’re not asking for a free ride,” Walker said. “We’re asking them not to change the rules in the middle of the game.”

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an investigative news piece explaining how Citibank and other credit card issuers are raising customer rates “any time, any reason,” using Rich Stevens of Merrick, New York, as the opening anecdote and covering proposed consumer protection bills.

**“Any Time, Any Reason”: How Credit Card Issuers Are Raising Rates on Customers Who Thought They Paid on Time**

*MERRICK, N.Y.* — When Rich Stevens opened the envelope from Citibank, he expected the usual: a monthly statement, a payment due date, maybe another promotional insert.

Instead, the Merrick, New York, resident found a notice that his credit card interest rate was going up — not because he had missed a payment with Citi, exceeded his credit limit, or bounced a check, but because the company said it had the right to change the terms of his account.

Like millions of cardholders, Stevens had learned the hard way that the interest rate printed on a credit card offer is not always the rate a customer keeps. Buried in card agreements and change-in-terms notices is a power that major issuers have increasingly used: the ability to raise rates on existing balances with little warning, often for broad reasons, and sometimes for no reason that the customer recognizes.

Consumer advocates have a name for it: “any time, any reason” repricing.

Banks call it risk management.

Either way, the result can be dramatic. A customer carrying a balance at 9.9 percent can suddenly find himself paying 19.99 percent, 24.99 percent, or more — even if he has never been late on that card.

## A Business Model Built on Moving Targets

Credit card issuers, including Citibank, Chase, Bank of America, Capital One, Discover, and others, have long argued that revolving credit is unsecured and risky. Unlike a mortgage or car loan, there is no house or vehicle to repossess if the borrower stops paying. Issuers say they must be able to adjust rates when a customer’s risk profile changes, when market conditions shift, or when funding costs rise.

But the practice has expanded far beyond traditional penalty pricing for missed payments.

In recent years, cardholders have reported rate increases triggered by:

- A late payment to a different creditor  
- A decline in credit score  
- High balances on other accounts  
- “Too many” open accounts  
- Market conditions  
- A periodic review of the account  
- Or simply a change in the issuer’s pricing policy  

In some cases, customers are told they can reject the new terms — but only by closing the account and paying off the balance under the old rate. That “choice” can itself damage a customer’s credit score by reducing available credit and increasing the percentage of credit used.

“It’s a trap door,” said one consumer advocate familiar with credit card complaints. “The customer thinks the deal is the rate they agreed to. The bank thinks the deal is whatever the bank later says it is.”

## The Fine Print That Makes It Legal

The key is the credit card agreement.

Most card contracts give issuers broad authority to modify terms with advance notice. The required notice period has historically been short, and the language can be opaque. A typical change-in-terms notice may state that the annual percentage rate, or APR, will increase unless the customer opts out by a certain date. Many customers overlook the notice or fail to understand that the increase may apply to balances they already incurred.

That retroactive feature is what most angers borrowers.

If a customer bought groceries, school supplies, or a washing machine at a 10 percent rate, consumer groups argue, the issuer should not later be able to charge 25 percent interest on that same purchase. Banks counter that credit cards are open-ended lines of credit, not fixed-rate installment loans, and that variable pricing is part of the contract.

The distinction is at the center of a growing fight in Washington.

## Citibank and the Industry Defense

Citibank, one of the nation’s largest credit card issuers, has been among the companies criticized by customers and lawmakers for aggressive repricing practices. The bank has maintained, as the industry generally has, that rate changes are disclosed to customers and reflect the cost and risk of extending unsecured credit.

The American Bankers Association and other industry representatives have warned that restricting repricing could force issuers to raise rates for everyone, reduce credit limits, eliminate rewards, or deny cards to riskier borrowers. They argue that flexible pricing allows banks to offer credit to a broad range of consumers.

But critics say that argument ignores how card issuers market low rates to attract customers, then reserve the right to raise those rates after balances are built.

“The bank gets the customer in the door with one promise, then changes the price after the customer is already carrying debt,” said a congressional aide involved in credit card legislation. “That is not a competitive market. That is a captive market.”

## Universal Default: Punished by One Bank for Another Bill

One of the most controversial tools is known as **universal default**.

Under universal default, a card issuer may raise a customer’s APR because of a late payment or negative mark involving an entirely different lender — a utility bill, another credit card, an auto loan, or even an error on a credit report.

The practice rests on the idea that financial distress in one account signals risk in others. But consumer advocates say it punishes borrowers twice and can create a spiral: one late payment leads to higher rates, which makes minimum payments harder to meet, which leads to more delinquencies.

For customers like Stevens, the most frustrating part is the lack of a clear connection between behavior and punishment. A borrower can make every required payment to a credit card company and still face a rate hike based on information outside that relationship.

## Minimum Payments, Maximum Interest

Rate increases are especially costly because many cardholders pay only the minimum amount due. A higher APR can add years to repayment and thousands of dollars in interest.

For example, a $5,000 balance at 10 percent interest is burdensome but manageable for many families. At 25 percent, the same balance becomes far more difficult to retire, especially if new fees or penalty rates are added.

Consumer lawyers say the business model encourages long-term indebtedness. Low minimum payments keep accounts current, but they also keep interest flowing. When rates rise, the portion of a payment going toward principal shrinks.

That dynamic is particularly harmful to households using credit cards as a financial bridge — for medical bills, car repairs, job loss, or rising gas and food prices.

## Lawmakers Move to Rein In the Practice

The growing backlash has produced several proposed consumer protection bills in Congress.

Among the most prominent proposals is the **Credit Cardholders’ Bill of Rights**, which would restrict some of the most criticized practices in the industry. Versions of the legislation have sought to:

- Prohibit arbitrary interest rate increases on existing balances  
- Require clearer advance notice before rate changes  
- Limit retroactive application of new rates  
- Ban or restrict universal default  
- Require payments above the minimum to be applied first to balances with the highest interest rates  
- Prevent due-date tricks, such as weekend or midday deadlines that trigger late fees  
- Require more transparent billing and disclosure  

Another proposal, often discussed under the banner of stopping unfair credit card practices, would give federal regulators greater authority to police abusive terms and require issuers to provide meaningful opt-out rights.

Supporters say these bills would restore a basic principle: the price of debt already incurred should not change unless the borrower violates the agreement.

Opponents warn that the bills could reduce credit availability and increase upfront costs. If issuers cannot reprice risky accounts, they say, banks will compensate by charging higher initial rates, annual fees, or tighter credit limits.

## Regulators Under Pressure

Federal regulators have also faced pressure to act. The Federal Reserve, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, and other banking agencies have been urged to treat retroactive rate hikes and universal default as unfair or deceptive practices.

For years, critics say, regulators relied too heavily on disclosure — the idea that if a practice is described in fine print, it is acceptable. But consumer advocates argue that disclosure does not solve the problem when the terms are complex, one-sided, and subject to change.

“Consumers cannot shop effectively when the price can be changed after the purchase,” said one advocate. “That is the central flaw in the credit card market.”

## The Human Cost Behind the Notices

For Rich Stevens, the issue is not an abstract debate about banking regulation. It is about trust.

He believed that paying on time meant keeping the bargain. The bank viewed the bargain differently: the account terms allowed it to reassess the rate.

That gap — between what consumers think they agreed to and what issuers legally reserve the right to do — is driving the political fight.

As more Americans rely on credit cards to cover everyday expenses, the stakes are rising. A rate increase is not just a number on a statement. It can determine whether a family gets out of debt or falls deeper into it.

The proposed bills in Washington may not eliminate high interest rates. They may not stop banks from pricing for risk. But they would challenge one of the industry’s most powerful tools: the ability to change the cost of yesterday’s purchases based on today’s decision.

For cardholders like Stevens, that reform cannot come soon enough.

# Consumers cry foul over credit card “rate-jacking”

**By Staff Writer**  
**WASHINGTON (CNN-style report)**

Angry credit card customers are pushing back against a practice they call “rate-jacking” — sudden increases in interest rates on existing balances, often with little warning and even when cardholders say they have paid on time.

The outrage has intensified as major banks face scrutiny over taxpayer support during the financial crisis. Citigroup, one of the nation’s largest credit card issuers, received a $20 billion federal bailout, fueling consumer complaints that banks benefiting from public funds should not be sharply raising rates on struggling households.

Consumer advocates say card issuers have used broad contract language to raise annual percentage rates, reduce credit limits or change payment terms based on factors that may have little to do with a customer’s record with that particular card. Many cardholders say the higher rates make it harder to pay down debt, trapping them in a cycle of mounting finance charges.

On Capitol Hill, Rep. Carolyn Maloney, D-New York, has pushed a “Credit Cardholders’ Bill of Rights,” aimed at limiting sudden interest-rate hikes, requiring clearer disclosures and restricting practices such as applying payments in ways that maximize finance charges. Supporters say the legislation would bring basic fairness to a market where consumers often discover major changes only after they arrive in the mail.

In the Senate, Sen. Christopher Dodd, D-Connecticut, has backed similar consumer protections, but his bill has stalled amid opposition from the banking industry and competing legislative priorities. Banks argue that they need flexibility to manage risk, especially during an economic downturn when defaults are rising.

The Federal Reserve also may step in. Regulators have been considering rules to curb some of the most controversial credit card practices, including retroactive rate increases and billing methods that consumer groups say are unfair or deceptive.

For many consumers, the issue is simple: If taxpayers are helping stabilize banks, they say, banks should not be allowed to squeeze customers with sudden rate increases.

Lawmakers and regulators now face growing pressure to decide whether voluntary industry changes are enough — or whether federal rules are needed to stop credit card rate-jacking.
